conclusion.justification: The report concludes that the claim is plausible but overstated, noting that while a vegetarian diet may modestly improve survival and lower cardiovascular mortality, the evidence regarding overall life expectancy is inconsistent, observational, and insufficient to establish causality due to confounding factors. Thus, it treats the evidence as insufficient and balanced.

report:
Bottom line: the claim is **plausible but overstated**. Vegetarian patterns are consistently linked to lower ischemic-heart-disease risk, but evidence that they directly extend life expectancy is observational, inconsistent for all-cause mortality, and vulnerable to “healthy user” confounding.

In Adventist Health Study 2, all vegetarians combined had lower all-cause mortality than nonvegetarians (adjusted HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.80–0.97), with stronger signals in men; however, Adventists differ in smoking, alcohol, exercise, and community factors, so causality is limited: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/1710093

A broader meta-analysis found vegetarian diets reduced ischemic-heart-disease mortality but had **no clear effect on all-cause or cerebrovascular mortality**, with low certainty of evidence: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/

EPIC-Oxford adds nuance: vegetarians/vegans had lower ischemic heart disease risk but higher hemorrhagic and total stroke risk, showing trade-offs rather than a simple longevity win: https://www.oxfordmartin.ox.ac.uk/publications/risks-of-ischaemic-heart-disease-and-stroke-in-meat-eaters-fish-eaters-and-vegetarians

A 2024 AJCN analysis reports protective associations for all-cause mortality in vegetarian Adventists, but still within the same confounding-prone cohort context: https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(24)00652-X/fulltext

Conclusion: a well-planned vegetarian diet may lower cardiovascular mortality and could modestly improve survival, especially versus processed/red-meat-heavy diets, but current evidence does **not** prove that simply avoiding meat increases life expectancy. Diet quality, lifestyle, and socioeconomic factors likely explain much of the association.
